summary: Mike Phipps frames the core strategic question: as AI commoditizes models, frontends, and agent frameworks, what remains defensible? His answer is the data model and tacit knowledge of internal processes. The Gates Foundation rolled out SIP (Strategic Intelligence Platform) enterprise-wide across ~4,000 people, modeling 25+ years of grantmaking ($7B annual disbursement, 2,000+ grants/year, 100+ countries, 80+ strategy teams). The architecture flows from siloed systems of record into a data lakehouse, through a curation layer (filtering, dedup, semantic chunking, field extraction, tagging, figure-to-text conversion), governed for PII masking and entitlements, into a Neo4j knowledge graph served to agents via MCP. The graph models multiple hierarchies: an additive DAG for funding (5 levels, funds→portfolios→investments→transactions) and a management hierarchy with derived rollup_manages edges. A third hierarchy models people—owners, attendees, directors, reporting structures—stitching across siloed HR and other source systems via common entities. Unstructured documents (meetings, reports) are chunked into semantic sections with full-text indexes, connected back to the organizational structure, enabling both graph retrieval and text search. The full model interconnects four different source systems into one semantic layer exposed through MCP. The chat UI is not defensible; users already have ChatGPT, so SIP serves them where they are. Constrained workflow experiences via MCP apps and sandboxed agents are being built alongside general chat. Retrieval evals use targeted questions matched to reporting standards, separated into complexity tiers, with live graph queries compared against agent answers at runtime. LLM-as-judge measures pass-at-one and stability; the feedback loop updates the data model, domain rules, and schema descriptions. Remaining misses tend to be ambiguously correct answers—not what the user intended. Future work includes filling out systems of record, expanding to enterprise-wide datasets, federated graph experiences for team-specific data, and additional agentic workflows.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: The durable moat is the data model plus tacit knowledge of how questions should be answered—not models, frontends, or agent frameworks.
Engaging data owners to capture reporting conventions, field semantics, join logic, and security trimmings is the core defensible work.
SIP models 25 years of Gates Foundation grantmaking ($7B/year, 2,000 grants, 4,000 employees) into one Neo4j knowledge graph served to Claude via MCP.
The graph is built for agent consumption—hierarchies become traversable paths, and unstructured documents connect to structured entities.
Multiple hierarchy types coexist: additive DAG for funding, level-specific management with derived rollup edges, and a people/org-chart hierarchy stitching siloed systems.
The chat UI is not defensible; SIP serves users where they already are (ChatGPT/general chat) and is building constrained MCP-based workflow experiences.
Retrieval evals with targeted questions, live graph query comparison, LLM-as-judge, and pass-at-one/stability metrics feed back into the data model and schema descriptions.
Remaining eval misses tend to be answers that are technically correct but not what the user intended—ambiguity is the constant struggle.
A small team's effort compounds in the data model layer; the modeling process itself reveals gaps in understanding.
Future directions include federated graph experiences for team-specific data and expanded agentic workflows.

sections.title: The moat question: what stays defensible as AI commoditizes
sections.summary: Phipps frames the strategic question of what remains defensible as AI commoditizes. Models, frontends, and agent frameworks can be quickly built but production brings constraints. The team's moat is understanding of internal processes and tacit knowledge needed for successful AI—durable regardless of new model releases or apps.

sections.title: SIP across the 4,000 person Gates Foundation
sections.summary: Introduces SIP (Strategic Intelligence Platform), just rolled out in production enterprise-wide across the Gates Foundation's ~4,000 people. It models tacit knowledge and internal processes into a graph.

sections.title: The scale: 25 years, $7B a year, 2,000 grants
sections.summary: Background on Gates Foundation scope: 25+ years, broad initiatives (child mortality, nutrition, agriculture, education), 2,000+ grants/year, 100+ countries, $7B annual disbursement, multiple divisions. The challenge is extracting insights from this structured data at scale.

sections.title: Structuring operational data for agentic retrieval
sections.summary: SIP structures operational data for agentic retrieval. Architecture: siloed systems of record → data lakehouse → curation layer → SIP cross-system semantic graph layer with agentic chat/workflow as UX. Built with agent as consumer, not dashboards.

sections.title: Tacit knowledge as the moat: engaging data owners
sections.summary: Engaging data owners is critical for capturing tacit knowledge: full field meanings, join logic, data limitations, systematics, security trimmings, reporting conventions. Questions must be answered the way they've been answered in the past. This procedural understanding is the moat.

sections.title: The curation pipeline and governance
sections.summary: Curation considerations: preprocessing, filtering, deduplication, document ordering, structured field extraction, semantic chunking for unstructured docs, figure-to-text conversion, tagging for graph connections, metadata as graph properties. Governance: PII masking, sensitive data classification, entitlements—risk sphere is larger with AI.

sections.title: Modeling hierarchies: funding and management lenses
sections.summary: Walkthrough of the data model. Entry point: 80+ strategy teams with annual reviews. First hierarchy is an additive DAG with 5 levels for funding: funds→portfolios→investments→transactions, with in_path shortcut edges. Multiple funding teams can fund one investment. Second hierarchy is management: each level matters independently, with contains and manages edges, plus derived rollup_manages edge for indirect management attribution. Two lenses (funding and management) exist for one investment.

sections.title: People, org charts, and stitching siloed systems
sections.summary: A third hierarchy models people—owners, meeting attendees, directors—with reporting structures and team structures. These traditionally lived only in HR source systems but are relevant to the full organizational story. Common entities across siloed source systems are stitched together so the agent can traverse a complicated organizational structure.

sections.title: Combining unstructured documents with structured data
sections.summary: Meetings have documents; documents have semantic sections/chunks with full-text indexes for search and retrieval. Pure graph retrieval is also available. All documents connect back to the main organizational structure. The full data model interconnects four source systems into one graph, one semantic layer exposed through MCP. The modeling process itself reveals gaps in understanding—valuable for developers.

sections.title: Serving the graph to Claude through MCP
sections.summary: The chat UI is not defensible; users already have ChatGPT. SIP serves the platform where users are via MCP, using a forked Neo4j MCP server with schema updates and state-passing modifications. General chat is one entry point; constrained workflow experiences via MCP apps and sandboxed agents are being built, pulling from the same knowledge graph backend.

sections.title: Retrieval evals and the feedback loop
sections.summary: Evals reveal data model gaps and ambiguities. Targeted eval questions match reporting standards, separated into complexity tiers. Live graph queries are compared against agent answers at runtime. LLM-as-judge measures pass-at-one and stability. Feedback loop updates data model, domain rules, and schema descriptions. Remaining misses are technically correct but not what the user intended. Future: fill out systems of record, expand to enterprise datasets, federated graph for team-specific data, additional agentic experiences.
